title: Ezekiel 32:17–32
context: Ezekiel 32:17–32 is dated to the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of a month the WEB text does not name, so many place it shortly after the previous oracle. The LORD tells the prophet to wail for the multitude of Egypt and send them down to the pit with the famous nations. The dirge pictures Sheol, the place of the dead, where Egypt joins those slain by the sword and lies among the uncircumcised. There lie Asshur, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians, each with their graves around them, each having caused terror in the land of the living and now bearing their shame. Pharaoh will see them and be comforted, for he too will lie among the slain. The repeated phrases about the uncircumcised and the slain mark dishonor in death; some note that Egyptians practiced circumcision, which would make this placement especially shameful, though the exact sense is debated. Both traditions read this dirge soberly as poetry about the end of human pride and violence, not as a detailed map of the afterlife.

verses.text: Also in the twelfth year, in the fifteenth day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports a word in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month. Arminians see this final Egypt oracle following closely after the previous one, completing the collection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Both traditions note that the WEB does not name the month here, so many place the oracle shortly after 32:1, and they hold the exact date loosely.

verses.text: “Son of man, wail for the multitude of Egypt, and cast them down, even her and the daughters of the famous nations, to the lower parts of the earth, with those who go down into the pit.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to wail for Egypt’s multitude and send them down to the pit with the famous nations. Arminian readers see the prophet’s words as a dirge that announces Egypt’s place among the fallen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the prophet’s lament as part of God’s word of judgment. Both traditions read the pit as poetic language for death and the grave, and they treat the dirge soberly.

verses.text: Whom do you pass in beauty? Go down, and be laid with the uncircumcised.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whom Egypt surpasses in beauty, and tells it to go down and lie with the uncircumcised. Arminians see Egypt’s pride in its beauty answered by its humiliation in death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as exposing Egypt’s pride. Both traditions note that lying among the uncircumcised marks dishonor, and some suggest it was especially shameful for Egypt, which practiced circumcision.

verses.text: They will fall among those who are slain by the sword. She is delivered to the sword. Draw her away with all her multitudes.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Egypt will fall among the slain, delivered to the sword, and be dragged away with its multitudes. Arminian readers see the certainty of Egypt’s fate, which matches that of other fallen nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice in Egypt’s fall. Both traditions read the verse as part of the dirge, sober in tone.

verses.text: The strong among the mighty will speak to him out of the middle of Sheol with those who help him. They have gone down. The uncircumcised lie still, slain by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the mighty in Sheol will speak to Pharaoh and his helpers, saying they have gone down and lie still among the uncircumcised. Arminians see poetic language picturing the dead greeting the newcomer, which stresses that death levels all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and compare a similar scene in Isaiah 14:9–10. Both traditions read Sheol, the place of the dead, as poetic setting rather than a detailed description of the afterlife.

verses.text: “Asshur is there with all her company. Her graves are all around her. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Asshur lies there with its company, its graves around it, all slain by the sword. Arminian readers see Assyria, the great empire of chapter 31, now pictured among the dead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reminder that even Assyria fell. Both traditions read the verse as beginning a list of fallen nations, each sharing the same end.

verses.text: whose graves are set in the uttermost parts of the pit, and her company is around her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who caused terror in the land of the living.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Assyria’s graves are in the depths of the pit, and those who caused terror in the land of the living are slain. Arminians see the link between violence in life and dishonor in death, which the dirge repeats.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice reaching even the mightiest. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and read the phrase caused terror as a key theme of the passage.

verses.text: “There is Elam and all her multitude around her grave; all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who have gone down uncircumcised into the lower parts of the earth, who caused their terror in the land of the living, and have borne their shame with those who go down to the pit.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Elam lies there with its multitude, slain and uncircumcised, bearing shame for the terror it caused. Arminian readers see another nation known for its power now humbled in death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the pattern repeated for each nation. Both traditions note that Elam lay east of Babylon, and they read its inclusion as showing the breadth of God’s judgment.

verses.text: They have made Elam a bed among the slain with all her multitude. Her graves are around her, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for their terror was caused in the land of the living, and they have borne their shame with those who go down to the pit. He is put among those who are slain.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Elam has been given a bed among the slain with its multitude, bearing its shame with those in the pit. Arminians see the repetition as emphasizing the certainty of Elam’s dishonor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as continuing the description of Elam. Both traditions treat the repetition as typical of lament poetry, reinforcing its sober tone.

verses.text: “There is Meshech, Tubal, and all their multitude. Their graves are around them, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for they caused their terror in the land of the living.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Meshech, Tubal, and their multitude lie there, uncircumcised and slain, for the terror they caused. Arminian readers see distant peoples included in the dirge, showing that judgment reaches every nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Meshech and Tubal appear again in Ezekiel 38–39. Both traditions locate them in Asia Minor, while holding the details with care.

verses.text: They will not lie with the mighty who are fallen of the uncircumcised, who have gone down to Sheol with their weapons of war and have laid their swords under their heads. Their iniquities are on their bones; for they were the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they will not lie with the fallen mighty ones who went down with weapons and swords under their heads. Arminians see a distinction between honored and dishonored burial, even among the dead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing degrees of dishonor in the poetry. Both traditions note that some translations read the verse as a question, and they treat the imagery as poetic rather than doctrinal.

verses.text: “But you will be broken among the uncircumcised, and will lie with those who are slain by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Pharaoh that he too will be broken among the uncircumcised and lie with the slain. Arminian readers see the dirge turning directly to Pharaoh, applying the fate of other nations to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as the focus of the catalog. Both traditions read it as the point toward which the whole list has been moving.

verses.text: “There is Edom, her kings, and all her princes, who in their might are laid with those who are slain by the sword. They will lie with the uncircumcised, and with those who go down to the pit.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Edom, its kings, and its princes lie with the slain, the uncircumcised, and those in the pit. Arminians see Edom, Judah’s neighbor and enemy, also humbled in death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice toward Edom (compare 25:12–14 and chapter 35). Both traditions read the verse as part of the sober catalog of fallen nations.

verses.text: “There are the princes of the north, all of them, and all the Sidonians, who have gone down with the slain. They are put to shame in the terror which they caused by their might. They lie uncircumcised with those who are slain by the sword, and bear their shame with those who go down to the pit.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the princes of the north and the Sidonians lie with the slain, put to shame for the terror they caused. Arminian readers see Phoenician cities and northern rulers joining the list, with the same verdict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the pattern of shame following violence. Both traditions note that the princes of the north are not further identified, and they avoid confident identifications.

verses.text: “Pharaoh will see them and will be comforted over all his multitude, even Pharaoh and all his army, slain by the sword,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over his multitude, for he and his army are slain. Arminians see a grim comfort, where Pharaoh finds only the company of other fallen powers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony of the comfort. Both traditions compare 31:16, where the trees of Eden were comforted, and read the image as poetic.

verses.text: “For I have put his terror in the land of the living. He will be laid among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, even Pharaoh and all his multitude,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he has put Pharaoh’s terror in the land of the living, and Pharaoh will lie among the uncircumcised and slain. Arminian readers see the final word of the Egypt oracles, which confirms that God governs both the rise and fall of nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty even over the terror Pharaoh caused. Both traditions read the verse as closing the collection with a sober reminder that all human pride ends in death before God.
